cf.title: pg_trgm: don't lose rows in index scans with a zero similarity threshold

input.subject: BUG #19701: GIN trigram index loses rows at similarity_threshold 0

verdict_reasoning: The proposal fixes a wrong-results bug in existing contrib opclasses, and no surviving objection questions the goal. The one surviving objection, standards-compat-1, is fixable: pgtrgm.sgml says "greater than" while the patch makes the indexes follow >=, and nobody has confirmed which meaning is intended. A committer who knows pg_trgm has to settle that and the back-patch decision.

brief.title: pg_trgm: make GIN and GiST scans return all rows at threshold 0
brief.problem: With a pg_trgm similarity threshold of 0, which the GUC and set_limit() accept, every row matches %, <% and <<%. GIN index scans return only rows sharing a trigram with the query, and return nothing for a query with no trigrams. GiST also loses rows on internal pages for such queries. Any user who sets a threshold of 0 gets silently wrong results from plans the planner picks itself.
brief.proposed_design: gin_extract_query_trgm() asks for GIN_SEARCH_MODE_ALL when the threshold is 0, as it already does for queries with no trigrams. The GIN consistent functions and the GiST consistent function on internal pages accept candidates when the query has no trigrams and the threshold is 0. v3 adds a separate 0001 that fixes an out-of-bounds read in calc_word_similarity() when neither string has a trigram.
user_visible_surface: Changed results: %, <%, <<% and commutators through gin_trgm_ops return every row at threshold 0, including rows sharing no trigram with the query.
Changed results: gin_trgm_ops and gist_trgm_ops return rows for a query with no trigrams (such as '' or '#') at threshold 0.
Changed plan cost in practice: at threshold 0 a GIN scan becomes a full index scan.
author_claims: The operators mean similarity >= threshold, so a threshold of 0 must match every row.
With default thresholds, all tested queries return the same rows as before.
Without the C changes the new regression tests fail; with them all pg_trgm tests pass, also under -fsanitize=undefined and cassert.
The patch applies cleanly to REL_14_STABLE through REL_19_STABLE; tests were run on master, REL_18_STABLE and REL_14_STABLE.
The calc_word_similarity() over-read also happens on master with word_similarity('', '') and never changes the result.
brief.thread_state: Palak Chaturvedi reviewed v1 and v2, compared row sets for all six operator forms, asked for more tests and called v2 good. Manu then posted v3 to fix a cfbot sanitizer failure; no one has replied to v3 and no committer has commented.
unclear: The reporter notes that pgtrgm.sgml says "greater than" while the code uses >=, but no documentation hunk appears in the touched files.
Nobody has confirmed which semantics is intended, so no one has ruled out changing the operators to > instead of fixing the indexes.
The proposal does not discuss the cost of a full GIN index scan at threshold 0, or whether users should be warned.
The patch prose shown covers only v1; the commit message and touched files of v3-0001 are not shown.
No committer has stated whether this is back-patched, which would change query results in minor releases.

objections.title: Patch fixes indexes to >= while pgtrgm.sgml still documents "greater than"
objections.failure_scenario: A user reads pgtrgm.sgml, which says % is true when similarity is "greater than" the threshold. The user sets the threshold to 0 to mean "any shared trigram". After the patch, every row comes back, including rows with similarity 0, and the documentation still describes the old meaning.
objections.argument: Message #1 states that the documented contract (>) and the implemented one (>=) differ, and that at threshold 0 this choice decides the whole outcome. The patch touches only trgm_gin.c, trgm_gist.c and tests, so it settles the semantics in code without changing the user-facing contract. The reporter's argument for >= is reasonable. But no reviewer or committer in the thread has confirmed it, and a committer would likely want the documentation changed in the same commit.
objections.author_must_show: Will the patch change pgtrgm.sgml to "greater than or equal to" for %, <% and <<%, and why is >= preferred over making 0 behave as documented?

critic.reasoning: The patch touches only trgm_gin.c, trgm_gist.c and the tests, while its commit message states the >= meaning that pgtrgm.sgml contradicts. Nobody in the thread has confirmed >= as the intended semantics, so the documentation change is still missing.

refuted.title: Back-patch changes rows and scan cost at threshold 0 in minor releases
refuted.failure_scenario: A site runs with pg_trgm.similarity_threshold = 0 and a GIN index, and today gets only rows that share a trigram. After a minor update to 14.x through 18.x, the same query returns the whole table through a full GIN index scan. The site finds out from slower queries and larger result sets, with no release note warning.
refuted.argument: Message #2 says the patch applies to REL_14_STABLE through REL_19_STABLE, but no committer has said whether to back-patch. Under the documented "greater than" wording, the current GIN behaviour matches the docs, so some users may depend on it. The proposal also does not discuss the cost of GIN_SEARCH_MODE_ALL at threshold 0. A committer would likely ask whether this belongs in master only, or needs a release note entry.
refuted.author_must_show: Should this be back-patched even though the documentation supports the current GIN results, and what release note would tell threshold-0 users their row counts and scan costs change?

critic.reasoning: The scenario describes the fix itself. A sequential scan and GiST already return every row at threshold 0, so today's GIN result depends on the plan and no site can rely on it. Any correct plan must read every row.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: The patch fixes the meaning of %, <% and <<% as >=, while pgtrgm.sgml documents "greater than".

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: At threshold 0 a GIN scan becomes a full index scan, and the proposal does not discuss its cost.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Message #2 says the patch applies to REL_14_STABLE through REL_19_STABLE; it changes query results at threshold 0 in minor releases.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Will the patch change pgtrgm.sgml to say "greater than or equal to" for %, <% and <<%, in the same commit?
Why is fixing the indexes to >= preferred over changing the operators to > so that threshold 0 behaves as documented?
Is the fix meant for back-patching to REL_14_STABLE and later, given that GIN results at threshold 0 change in a minor release?
What does v3-0001 touch, and should the calc_word_similarity() over-read fix be committed and back-patched separately from the index fix?
Should the documentation tell users that a GIN scan at threshold 0 reads the whole index?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the pg_trgm opclasses and the GIN and GiST consistent-function contracts, including GIN search modes.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the >= meaning of the three operators at threshold 0 in every supported branch, and for changed GIN and GiST results in minor releases if back-patched.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 after review and v3 after a cfbot sanitizer failure, which suggests the author stays for fixes.

priority.reason: Few users set a threshold of 0, but the planner picks plans that silently lose rows for those who do. The patch is small and has one review, but no committer has replied, and the semantics and back-patch decisions need one.

provisional_note: The code was not read, and the commit message and touched files of v3-0001 are not shown. Whether the consistent-function changes are correct for all strategies and for the GIN pending list could not be judged.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fillfactor for GIN indexes
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add fillfactor as a storage parameter for GIN indexes, controlling how full pages are packed at index build time and, in later versions, the split ratio of posting-tree pages. Revised versions applied fillfactor only to posting trees and debated whether the default should be 100 (matching 9.4 index sizes) or 90 (matching btree).
precedents_retrieved.objection: No test results or benchmarks were provided showing that a fillfactor parameter improves GIN index performance, although an earlier reviewer had asked for them and got no reply. Robert Haas objected on that basis. The author agreed that no such benchmark existed and that he had no time to work on it soon, and asked for the patch to be rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There's only value in adding a fillfactor parameter to GIN indexes if
it improves performance.  There are no benchmarks showing it does.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pageinspect - add functions on GIN and GiST indexes from gevel
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Alexander Korotkov, Tomas Vondra, Ashutosh Sharma, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the gevel module's functions for GiST, SP-GiST and GIN indexes into pageinspect, with tests and docs. The functions show whole-index statistics, print the tree and its stored objects, and estimate GIN value counts and query matches.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said the functions read the whole index, while pageinspect inspects single pages, so the code belongs in a new extension or should be rewritten as page-level functions. Peter Eisentraut also found that the patch no longer compiled and that the stats functions returned one formatted text value where they should return a row with columns. The author planned a new contrib module but posted no new version, and the entry was returned with feedback after three weeks of waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The proposed patch uses a very different approach, reading the whole index,
not individual pages. Why should it be part of pageinspect?

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in Gin index
precedents_retrieved.summary: A GSoC 2017 patch adding explicit predicate locking to the GIN index access method for serializable isolation, placing page-level predicate locks on entry tree and posting tree leaf pages and copying locks on page splits. It also handled conflict detection when fast update is enabled.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewer Alexander Korotkov found the locking scheme redundant and asked for changes: lock posting tree leaves instead of entry tree leaves, apply page-level locks only when fast update is off, add in-code comments, and improve the isolation tests so they actually create posting trees. After his last review the thread had no updates for almost two months, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This thread had no updates for almost two months, so I am marking it
as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in gin index
precedents_retrieved.summary: A GSoC 2017 patch adds explicit predicate locking to the GIN index access method so that serializable transactions detect rw-conflicts at page level. When fast update is on, the patch falls back to coarser locking.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund closed the entry as a duplicate of an older commitfest entry (1466), so it was not rejected on technical grounds. Before that, Michael Paquier had marked it returned with feedback after about two months with no update. Alexander Korotkov's review asked for consistent fast-update conditions, code comments, and isolation tests that build a posting tree.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This appears to be a duplicate of https://commitfest.postgresql.org/17/1466/ - as the other one is older, I'm closing this one.

precedents_retrieved.title: GIN fillfactor
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a fillfactor storage parameter to GIN indexes so that index build leaves free space on pages, and apply it to the page split ratio in dataPlaceToPageLeaf. The default was debated between 100, which matches the packed 9.4 indexes, and 90.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No benchmark showed that the option improves performance. Heikki Linnakangas tested random updates and found that GIN indexes do not bloat after build, because posting tree pages already keep some free space, so he concluded the option is not useful in practice. Alexander Korotkov showed one case with bloat but agreed it was probably not worth it without real use cases.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Based on this, I think we should just drop this patch. It's not useful in
practice.

precedents_retrieved.title: Don't allow to EXECUTE empty queries (fixes Assert violation)
precedents_retrieved.authors: Tom Lane (tgl), Aleksander Alekseev (a.alekseev), Alexander Lakhin (law)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch made the server raise an error on EXECUTE of an empty prepared statement, such as one created with psql \parse and no query text. This would stop the failed Assert on qc->commandTag in PortalRunMulti.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to throwing an error, because pre-v12 servers return the EXECUTE command tag for an empty prepared statement and non-assert builds still do. Tracing showed the outer Portal supplies the EXECUTE tag, so the Assert in PortalRunMulti was itself wrong. Álvaro Herrera's patch, which removes the Assert and rewrites the comment, was pushed instead.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Hmm, throwing an error is exactly not what I was suggesting above.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rename trim_array() for consistency with the rest of array_* functions
precedents_retrieved.summary: Rename trim_array() to array_trim() so it matches the array_* naming of other array functions and shows up in \df array_*. The old name would stay as an undocumented, deprecated alias, to be removed in about 10 years.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Vik Fearing pointed out that the SQL standard mandates TRIM_ARRAY(), so it cannot be deprecated. Michael Paquier suggested leaving things as they are on HEAD, since other functions are likely in the same position, and the author withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
While unfortunately named, we cannot deprecate TRIM_ARRAY() because it
is mandated by the standard.

precedents_retrieved.title: Extracting only the columns needed for a query
precedents_retrieved.summary: Have the planner compute, for each relation in a query, the set of columns that actually need to be scanned (a scanCols bitmap stored in RangeTblEntry, extracted in make_one_rel()), so table access methods such as zedstore can use it for costing and execution. Companion patches showed an extended ANALYZE API and a per-column disk-size statistic for using scanCols in cost estimation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The authors withdrew the entry themselves. They said they would post a new thread with a combined patch set: the scanCols patch, a patch to capture RETURNING columns, and patches passing the column list to table AM functions. Review had also found open issues, such as excess scanCols for DELETE ... USING ... RETURNING and for partitioned tables, which the authors said were tricky to fix within the current extraction logic. No reviewer objected to the approach.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Melanie and me will be posting a separate thread with the scanCols patch
listed here, a patch to capture the set of cols in RETURNING and a group
of patches to pass down the list of cols to various table AM functions
together as a patch set.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
Reverted commit(s): Compress GIN posting lists, for smaller index size.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 36a35c55 changed the divisor from 3 to 6, for no apparent reason.
Reducing GinMaxItemSize like that created a dump/reload hazard: loading a
9.3 database to 9.4 might fail with "index row size XXX exceeds maximum 1352
for index ..." error. Revert the change.

While we're at it, make the calculation slightly more accurate. It used to
divide the available space on page by three, then subtract
sizeof(ItemIdData), and finally round down. That's not totally accurate; the
item pointers for the three items are packed tight right after the page
header, but there is alignment padding after the item pointers. Change the
calculation to reflect that, like BTMaxItemSize does. I tested this with
different block sizes on systems with 4- and 8-byte alignment, and the value
after the final MAXALIGN_DOWN was the same with both methods on all
configurations. So this does not make any difference currently, but let's be
tidy.

Also add a comment explaining what the macro does.

This fixes bug #12292 reported by Robert Thaler. Backpatch to 9.4, where the
bug was introduced.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the retrieved list has no earlier rejected, returned or reverted proposal on this idea. Message #1 cites BUG #14202 (2016) as the fix that made gtrgm_consistent use >=, which supports the >= reading and is not a rejection. Other angles cover the semantics and back-patch questions.
Both objections concern the user-facing contract and can be fixed in a new version. The correctness fix itself raises no syntax, GUC, pg_dump or psql concern.

The patch only changes query-time logic in the GIN extract_query and consistent functions and the GiST consistent function. Index contents, WAL, catalogs, the wire protocol and extension-visible structs stay the same, so existing indexes need no rebuild after a minor update. A standby on an older minor release can return different index results during a rolling update, but that is the existing wrong-results bug, and a sequential scan on either node already returns the full set.

From the security angle there is nothing to object to. The threshold is a per-session setting, so the full GIN index scan at 0 costs only the session that sets it, and is no worse than a sequential scan it could already force. RLS and column privileges are unchanged, the operators' leakproofness is unchanged, and v3-0001 removes an over-read that did not change results. Back-patch effects on query results belong to other angles.

From the maintenance and fit angle there is nothing to object to. The patch fixes wrong results in existing contrib opclasses, touches only trgm_gin.c, trgm_gist.c and tests, and adds a small threshold check that has no cost at non-zero thresholds and creates no new API or ongoing work. The full GIN scan at threshold 0 costs only users who choose that threshold. Separate from the verdict: no committer has engaged yet, and the docs ('greater than' versus >=) and back-patching are not yet settled, which other angles cover.

No existing feature, option or extension gives correct index results for %, <% and <<% at threshold 0, so the need is not already met. This is a wrong-results bug in core contrib, and no workaround returns the rows a sequential scan returns. Leaving out the predicate or using a tiny positive threshold changes the query, and keeping the index means editing pg_trgm itself. The patch extends the GIN_SEARCH_MODE_ALL path that already exists for queries with no trigrams, so it adds no second mechanism. Whether to forbid 0 or switch the operators to > is a design question for other angles.

This is a wrong-results bug fix, and the demand test does not apply in the usual way. Threshold 0 is a legal value of the GUC and of set_limit(), and message #1 shows the planner picking a GIN plan on its own that returns 0 rows instead of 1. Message #2 confirms the bug on master, and a second person compared row sets in message #3. The extra cost of a full GIN scan falls only on sessions that set threshold 0. No other user pays for it. Few people may use threshold 0, but an index that changes query results is still a defect. Whether to fix the indexes or forbid 0 is a design question for other angles.
